name: Score Generation and Composition
title: Score Generation and Composition
answer: Score generation and composition covers the use of AI to create, extend, or arrange musical material for film, television, games, advertising, and concert works. This includes generating melodies, chord progressions, counterpoint, orchestration, full scores, MIDI performances, and finished audio stems. The field spans tools that output notation for live players, synthetic mockups for directors, and hybrid cues that blend human and machine writing. The site tracks 2000 audio models, many of which address some part of this scoring pipeline.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Most score generation tools run either as cloud services accessed through a web browser or as local plugins inside a digital audio workstation such as Ableton Live, Logic Pro, or Cubase. They typically require a modern GPU for local inference, though many composers use remote servers to avoid buying dedicated hardware. Output is usually delivered as MIDI, MusicXML, or audio files that drop into an existing session alongside sample libraries and notation software. Some systems also expose an API so that game engines or media servers can request music in real time.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A composer often begins with a short sketch, a reference track, or a text prompt describing mood, tempo, and instrumentation. The model then generates a set of candidate phrases, full cues, or orchestrations, which the composer auditions and edits in a piano roll or score editor. Many workflows use iterative prompting, where the composer keeps the best bars and asks the model to regenerate the rest, or uses stem separation to isolate and replace individual instruments. The final result is almost always a hybrid: the human fixes timing, dynamics, and voice leading while the machine supplies raw material and variations.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights in AI-generated scores are unsettled, and ownership often depends on the tool's terms of service, the training data, and the degree of human authorship. Of the 92 active intellectual property lawsuits tracked by this site, 18 involve AI music services, which shows how contested the area is. Composers should check whether a model was trained on licensed or public domain scores, because unlicensed training data can expose a production to infringement claims. Clear provenance records, split sheets, and contracts that assign AI output rights are becoming standard practice for sync and broadcast work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Score generation is moving toward real-time adaptive systems that respond to gameplay, scene changes, or listener context without a human triggering each cue. Models are also getting better at following detailed notation constraints, such as exact key signatures, instrument ranges, and articulation marks, which will make them more useful for concert composers. Expect tighter integration with notation editors and DAWs, where a composer can ask for a contrapuntal variation or a reorchestration directly on a selected passage. The likely outcome is not a replacement for composers but a faster sketching and arrangement layer that leaves final creative decisions to the human.
